question: Compare the top three open-source vector databases for a startup building RAG products.
stop_detail: All required criteria have supporting evidence.

short_answer.text: Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate are all open source, can be self-hosted, and support hybrid search. The clearest difference is operational: a distributed Milvus deployment depends on etcd, object storage, and a message queue. An independent benchmark found that no engine led on every dataset, so the choice should follow your own data, filters, and team capacity rather than a ranking.

key_findings.text: Milvus is an open-source vector database released under the Apache License 2.0.
Filtering during the vector search, rather than after it, avoids returning fewer results than requested when filters are selective.
An independent team found all three databases straightforward to start on a single machine with Docker.
The benchmark compared Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate on the same hardware, and none of the vendors funded or reviewed the study.
For a small team, the number of moving parts in a cluster may matter more than raw query speed when choosing among the three.
Qdrant's own published benchmarks report high throughput on the datasets Qdrant tested.

cells.text: Qdrant is licensed under Apache 2.0 and can be self-hosted with Docker or Kubernetes.
Qdrant supports hybrid search that combines dense and sparse vectors in one query.
In distributed mode, Qdrant shards collections and replicates them across nodes.
Milvus is an open-source vector database released under the Apache License 2.0.
Milvus supports hybrid search across multiple vector fields, including sparse vectors for keyword-style matching.
Milvus can run embedded as Milvus Lite, as a single-node standalone server, or as a distributed cluster.
Weaviate is an open-source vector database written in Go and released under the BSD 3-Clause license.
Weaviate's hybrid search combines BM25 keyword search with vector search.
Weaviate scales horizontally by sharding collections across nodes, with per-collection replication.
